statement: In 11 adults who used methamphetamine regularly, mainly by snorting it, and were not seeking treatment (one double-blind, placebo-controlled inpatient laboratory study in which each person had placebo and three single doses on separate days in counterbalanced order), a single intranasal dose taken earlier the same day, compared with placebo, is associated with shorter and worse sleep that night. After the highest dose, wrist activity monitors (worn by 6 of the 11) recorded about 2 hours less sleep (4.4 against 6.4 hours) and more awakenings; the two lower doses did not significantly change measured sleep. People's own estimates (all 11) were about 2.9 and 4.9 hours less sleep after the two higher doses, with worse ratings of falling asleep, sleeping well and waking often; the authors read the gap between reported and measured sleep as self-reports overstating the loss, a comparison that mixes 11 people's reports with 6 people's monitors. Single laboratory doses differ from the repeated doses and binges of everyday use, which the study did not test. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In a small hospital study, people slept less and worse on the night after a single dose of methamphetamine taken earlier that day than after a dummy dose. With the highest dose, a wrist monitor showed about two hours less sleep and more waking. People felt they had lost even more sleep than the monitor showed. Only 11 people took part, the monitor worked for 6 of them, and repeated doses or binges were not tested.
population: Adults aged 22 to 45 (2 women, 9 men) with DSM-IV methamphetamine abuse or dependence who used it mainly intranasally, were not seeking treatment and had no other psychiatric disorder; studied as inpatients
exposure: A single intranasal dose of methamphetamine given by the researchers earlier the same day (three dose levels; amounts and times are study conditions in the study card)
outcome: Sleep that night: total sleep and awakenings by wrist actigraphy (6 people); estimated hours slept and sleep-quality ratings the next morning (11 people)
magnitude: Actigraphy, highest dose against placebo: 4.4 against 6.4 hours of sleep (an average 2 hours less, p < .01) and more awakenings than after any other condition (p < .01); lower doses not significant. Self-estimated sleep: 7.70 (SEM 0.31) hours after placebo, 6.77 (0.56), 4.83 (0.85) and 2.84 (0.89) after the three active doses, about 2.9 and 4.9 hours less after the two higher doses (p < .001); 'slept well' 85.2 after placebo against 49.6 and 21.4, and 'woke often' 16.5 against 64.8 and 67.6 (100-point scales). No confidence intervals are reported.

evidence.locator: Results › 3.1 Sleep, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 legend (left panels, n = 6)
evidence.extracted: Actigraphy in 6 participants: total sleep after the highest dose 4.4 hours against 6.4 hours after placebo, an average reduction of 2 hours (p < .01); awakenings more frequent after the highest dose than after any other condition (p < .01).

evidence.locator: Results › 3.1 Sleep, 2nd paragraph; Table 1, sleep questionnaire rows
evidence.extracted: All 11 participants: estimated hours slept 7.70 (SEM 0.31) after placebo against 4.83 (0.85) and 2.84 (0.89) after the two higher doses, about 2.9 and 4.9 hours less (p < .001); 'fell asleep easily' 57.50 against 27.40 and 10.22; 'slept well' 85.20 against 49.60 and 21.44; 'woke often' 16.50 against 64.80 and 67.56; 'satisfied with sleep' 80.30 against 42.40 and 25.33 (df 1 and 30).

Actigraphy data were lost for the first five participants through equipment malfunction, so objective sleep comes from 6 of 11. The authors contrast nearly 5 fewer self-reported hours with 2 fewer measured hours and note that only single doses were studied, while illicit use, anecdotally, comes in multiple dose cycles that may continue over several consecutive days.

risk_of_bias.note: Counterbalanced order (scheme not described); blinding of a noticeable drug not checked, which matters for the self-rated sleep; actigraphy lost in 5 of 11 through equipment failure.

indirectness.note: Worded for the doses, route and setting studied.

imprecision.note: Eleven people (6 with actigraphy), one study, no confidence intervals.

grade.reasoning: A placebo-controlled within-person laboratory study with counterbalanced order starts high. Risk of bias -1 (order scheme not described; blinding not checked for self-rated outcomes; objective sleep missing in 5 of 11). Imprecision -2 (one study of 11 people, objective sleep in 6, no intervals). Very low. Not downgraded for indirectness because the claim is worded for single laboratory doses in experienced people and says that binges were not tested. Single study; the same participants appear in the acute-effects report of the same group, which is not independent evidence.
